lessons.title: SEC, Trading Hours, and Settlement: How US Market Rules Compare With SEBI's

children.text: In May 2024, the United States moved its stock market to T+1 settlement, meaning trades settle the next business day. India had already completed that move in January 2023, more than a year earlier. In August 2026, the flow went the other way: NSE borrowed Wall Street's closing auction to set end-of-day prices for F&O stocks. And in December 2026, Nasdaq plans to trade 23 hours a day, five days a week. Rules in the world's two most talked-about markets are converging and diverging at the same time. If you follow US stocks, or ever plan to buy them, you need to know where the rulebooks match and where they do not.

body.text: The US and India share the same goals: fair prices, safe settlement and honest disclosure. They reach them through different plumbing. The differences in hours, settlement, custody and investor protection decide what can go wrong for you and who covers it.

markDefs.definition: Self-regulatory organisation. A body that sets and enforces rules for its own members under the oversight of a government regulator. In the US, FINRA and the exchanges are SROs. In India, stock exchanges also perform front-line regulation of their members.

children.text: The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) was created by the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, after the 1929 crash. SEBI got its statutory powers under the SEBI Act of 1992, after the Harshad Mehta scam. Both are the top regulator, but the US leans more heavily on
. FINRA, a private body, writes and enforces most day-to-day rules for US brokers. In India, SEBI regulates brokers directly, with the exchanges supervising their own members.

children.text: Trading Hours: When Each Market Is Open

markDefs.definition: Trading outside regular hours, in the pre-market session before the open and the after-hours session after the close. Volumes are thinner and price swings can be larger.

children.text: The US regular session runs from 9:30 am to 4:00 pm Eastern Time, six and a half hours, against NSE's six and a quarter. But the US also has long

sessions: pre-market from 4:00 am and after-hours until 8:00 pm Eastern. Most US companies release results outside regular hours, so a lot of the big price moves happen when liquidity is thinnest. Converting to IST also depends on the season, because the US shifts its clocks and India does not.

body.caption: US trading sessions in Eastern Time and IST

Followed by the Closing Auction Session

body.label: Nasdaq's move to near round-the-clock trading
body.value: 23 hours a day, 5 days a week
body.context: Approved by the SEC on 10 April 2026. Nasdaq and NYSE Arca are targeting Sunday, 6 December 2026, with sessions from 9:00 pm Eastern to 8:00 pm Eastern the next day, subject to market data systems being ready.

body.title: Convert the new session to IST
body.textWithBlank: In December 2026, the US is on standard time and IST is 10 hours 30 minutes ahead of Eastern Time. Nasdaq's 23-hour session starting at 9:00 pm Eastern on Sunday begins at ___ IST on Monday.
body.explanation: 9:00 pm Eastern plus 10 hours 30 minutes is 7:30 am IST the next day. The session ends at 8:00 pm Eastern, which is 6:30 am IST. So from December, US-listed stocks on Nasdaq would be tradeable almost all day in Indian time, with a one-hour break from 6:30 am to 7:30 am IST.

body.text: Longer hours do not mean better prices. Outside the regular session, fewer participants are active, bid-ask spreads widen and a single large order can move the price sharply. Always use limit orders in pre-market, after-hours or overnight sessions. A market order at 3:00 am IST on thin volume can fill far from the last price you saw.

markDefs.definition: The number of business days between a trade and the final exchange of shares and money. T+1 means the trade date plus one business day.

children.text: matters because until a trade settles, money and shares are at risk if something goes wrong. Shorter cycles mean less risk and faster access to your funds. This is one area where India is genuinely ahead of the US. India completed its shift to T+1 in January 2023 and has since added an optional same-day T+0 cycle for the top 500 stocks. The US moved to T+1 only in May 2024.

body.title: Who got there first?
body.question: Which statement about settlement cycles is correct as of September 2026?
options: The US moved to T+1 before India and India is still on T+2
Both markets moved to T+1 on the same day in May 2024
India completed T+1 in January 2023 and offers optional T+0 for top stocks, while the US moved to T+1 in May 2024
The US settles on T+0 while India settles on T+1
body.explanation: India completed its T+1 transition in January 2023, well ahead of the US move on 28 May 2024. India also runs an optional T+0 cycle for the top 500 stocks, running alongside T+1. The US has no equivalent same-day cycle for regular trades.

markDefs.definition: When shares are registered in the name of your broker, or a nominee of the central depository, rather than in your own name. You remain the beneficial owner, and your broker's records show the shares belong to you.

children.text: When you buy Infosys on Zerodha, the shares land in a demat account in your own name at CDSL or NSDL, and you get a statement directly from the depository. When an American buys Apple on a US app, the shares are usually held in

. The central depository's nominee holds them, and the broker's books record that they belong to you. Both systems work, but they create different kinds of risk, which is why the two countries protect investors differently.

body.title: Custody and protection: US vs India

columns.label: United States
points: Shares typically held in street name through the broker and DTC
Broker records are the main proof of your ownership
Fractional shares widely offered by brokers
SIPC covers up to $500,000 per customer, including up to $250,000 in cash, if a member broker fails
SIPC does not cover losses from falling share prices

columns.label: India
points: Shares held in your own demat account at CDSL or NSDL
Depositories send you statements directly, independent of your broker
Fractional ownership of listed shares is not permitted
Exchange Investor Protection Funds compensate eligible claims if a broker defaults, up to ₹35 lakh per investor at NSE

body.title: Compare the safety nets
body.prompt: SIPC protection is up to $500,000 per customer. At USD/INR 95, what is that in ₹ lakh? Then compare it with NSE's Investor Protection Fund limit of ₹35 lakh. Enter the SIPC limit in ₹ lakh.
body.explanation: $500,000 × 95 = ₹4,75,00,000, which is ₹475 lakh or ₹4.75 crore. That is about 13.6 times NSE's ₹35 lakh limit. But the systems protect against different risks. Indian investors hold shares in their own demat accounts, so a broker failure mainly puts cash and pledged securities at risk, while US investors rely more on broker records.

children.text: Guardrails Compared: Circuit Breakers, Shorting and Day Trading

cells: Based on the S&P 500: 7% (Level 1) and 13% (Level 2) falls halt trading for 15 minutes if before 3:25 pm; 20% (Level 3) halts for the day
Based on Nifty 50 or Sensex: 10%, 15% and 20% falls trigger halts, with duration depending on the time of day
Limit Up-Limit Down bands pause a stock that moves too fast
Daily price bands of 2%, 5%, 10% or 20% for non-F&O stocks; dynamic bands for F&O stocks
Allowed; broker must locate borrowable shares first
Allowed for all investors, but naked short selling is banned; institutions disclose upfront, retail investors by end of day

body.caption: The index level at which a market-wide halt is triggered

body.title: Find the Level 1 trigger
body.prompt: The S&P 500 closed at 7,656.98 on 11 September 2026. At what index level would a Level 1 market-wide circuit breaker (a 7% fall) be triggered the next trading day? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Trigger = 7,656.98 × (1 − 0.07) = 7,656.98 × 0.93 = 7,120.99. If the S&P 500 fell to 7,120.99 before 3:25 pm Eastern, trading across US exchanges would halt for 15 minutes. India's first threshold is wider, at 10%, but the logic is the same.

body.text: Proposals are not rules. The SEC's May 2026 plan to let companies report every six months instead of every quarter was only a proposal, with comments due by 6 July 2026. Until a final rule is adopted, US companies continue filing quarterly 10-Q reports. When you read about a regulatory change, always check whether it is proposed, approved or already in effect.

body.title: An after-hours earnings night
body.scenario: You live in Pune and hold US shares through an overseas brokerage account. It is late October, so the US is still on daylight saving time. A US company you own reports results at 4:05 pm Eastern. By 2:00 am IST, its shares are down 9% in after-hours trading on very low volume. You are tempted to place a market sell order immediately. You also wonder whether your shares are safe if your US broker ever collapses.
body.prompt: Walk through what you should consider before placing the order, and explain how your shares are held and protected compared with your Indian holdings.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Timing: 4:05 pm Eastern is 1:35 am IST in daylight saving time. After-hours trading runs until 5:30 am IST, and the regular session opens at 7:00 pm IST.
2. Liquidity: After-hours volume is thin, so a market order could fill well below the displayed price. Use a limit order, or wait for the regular session when liquidity returns.
3. Price discovery: A 9% after-hours move on low volume can partly reverse by the regular open. Read the results before reacting.
4. Settlement: If you sell, the trade settles on T+1, so proceeds are available one business day later.
5. Custody: Your US shares are most likely held in street name through the broker and DTC, unlike your Indian shares, which sit in your own demat account at CDSL or NSDL.
6. Protection: If the US broker is a SIPC member and fails, SIPC covers up to $500,000, including $250,000 in cash. Neither SIPC nor India's Investor Protection Funds cover losses from a falling share price.
7. Separately, remember that overseas investing from India involves LRS limits and Indian tax rules, which are covered in a dedicated course.

body.title: Before you trade a US stock from India
steps: Check whether the US is on daylight saving or standard time and convert all session timings to IST.
Use limit orders for any trade outside the regular session.
Confirm your overseas broker is a SIPC member on sipc.org and understand how your shares are held.
Know that US trades settle on T+1 and plan when your cash will be available.
Check whether any rule you have read about, such as semiannual reporting, is proposed or actually in force.

cards.definition: US Securities and Exchange Commission, created in 1934. The top US securities regulator, chaired by Paul Atkins since April 2025.
A self-regulatory organisation that writes and enforces day-to-day rules for US brokers under SEC oversight.
US pre-market (from 4:00 am Eastern) and after-hours (until 8:00 pm Eastern) sessions, with thinner liquidity.
NSE's auction from 3:15 pm to 3:35 pm that sets the closing price of F&O stocks, live since 3 August 2026.
Settlement one business day after the trade. India completed it in January 2023, the US in May 2024.
Shares registered in a broker's or depository nominee's name on your behalf, the norm in the US.
Securities Investor Protection Corporation. Covers up to $500,000, including $250,000 in cash, if a member US broker fails. Does not cover market losses.
A trading halt triggered by a large index fall: 7%, 13% and 20% on the S&P 500 in the US; 10%, 15% and 20% on the Nifty 50 or Sensex in India.

points: The SEC (1934) and SEBI (statutory powers from 1992) are the top regulators, but the US relies more on self-regulatory bodies like FINRA.
US regular hours are 9:30 am to 4:00 pm Eastern, which is 7:00 pm to 1:30 am IST in summer and 8:00 pm to 2:30 am IST in winter, with long pre-market and after-hours sessions.
Nasdaq and NYSE Arca are targeting 23-hour weekday trading from 6 December 2026, after SEC approval in April 2026.
NSE introduced a Closing Auction Session for F&O stocks on 3 August 2026, and extended equity derivatives trading to 3:40 pm.
India led on settlement: T+1 completed in January 2023 plus optional T+0 for the top 500 stocks. The US reached T+1 in May 2024.

Indian shares sit in your own demat account; US shares are usually held in street name. SIPC covers up to $500,000 per customer, while NSE's Investor Protection Fund covers up to ₹35 lakh per investor.
The US scrapped its $25,000 Pattern Day Trader rule from 4 June 2026. Its circuit breakers trigger at 7%, 13% and 20%, compared with India's 10%, 15% and 20%.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or tax advice. Rules and timings are drawn from the SEC, FINRA, SIPC, SEBI, NSE and published reports as of September 2026 and can change. Investing overseas from India is subject to LRS limits and Indian tax rules. Always confirm current rules with your broker and the relevant regulator.
